entries.title: The AI Backlash Gets Professional
entries.summary: A new group is targeting tech companies and the government with the climate movement’s playbook.
entries.content:
A new group is targeting tech companies and the government with the climate movement’s playbook.

If there’s one thing America seems to agree on, it’s AI. Some three-quarters of Americans oppose a data center being built in their area, three-quarters of Americans think AI will hurt their job security, nearly 70 percent think the technology is advancing too quickly—the polls go on. Progressive and Republican candidates alike are bashing the tech industry to win primary elections. States and cities are halting plans for data-center development.

Yet in cloistered San Francisco, where I live, staffers at OpenAI and Anthropic are developing this same feared technology at light speed and pulling down compensation packages that stretch to considerably more than $1 million. Silicon Valley’s growth is largely unencumbered by regulation, and President Trump’s administration has if anything used its authority to speed the AI industry along. The divide between these camps—the majority of people in this country who simply have to deal with the technology as it’s rolled out, and the much smaller population of people with direct influence over it—is a defining feature of this era. And so I noticed when a small group, with ties to both the Bay Area and Washington, started making noise, insisting that the AI race slow down and the technology be overseen not by executives and engineers, but by the broadest population possible.

The group—which formally launched today and calls itself Irreplaceable, as in people are irreplaceable by machines—has an audacious and perhaps naive vision. It is essentially a protest against capitalism as it is practiced in America today, focused on resisting first and developing a coherent plan for the future later. I have seen exactly how bulletproof the AI companies are—pilfering seemingly infinite volumes of media to train their models, building unpermitted power plants for their data centers, and unleashing autonomous agents capable of massive security breaches, almost entirely without consequence. I wanted to meet with Irreplaceable’s founders to ask: How do they possibly expect to pull this off?

The organization is staffed with people who made a name for themselves in the climate movement, and they are hoping to avoid past mistakes by focusing on the emotional reaction Americans are having to AI, rather than anchoring their work in white papers and policy recommendations. “People get it,” Jeremy Ornstein—a campaign strategist for Irreplaceable and former organizer with the Sunrise Movement—told me. “People have the intuition that if we create machines more powerful than people, that could go dangerously and terribly wrong.”

Phil Aroneanu, Irreplaceable’s executive director and a co-founder of the climate organization 350.org, told me he believes that climate advocates initially floundered because they acted as policy wonks. They thought that making evidence-based arguments about the dangers of melting ice sheets and rising sea levels to receptive congresspeople would be enough to pass nationwide climate legislation. Today, Aroneanu said, movements are built not necessarily on what people think, but instead on what they feel. For climate, that meant fossil-fuel-divestment campaigns, protesting oil pipelines, and the school strikes led by Greta Thunberg. People are already “feeling the squeeze,” Aroneanu told me. “And we should be pointing that anxiety and that anger in the right direction.”

Irreplaceable will prioritize a range of issues: mitigating automation’s effects on the economy, protecting against government and corporate use of AI to surveil Americans, and establishing industry oversight and guardrails to prevent catastrophic disasters, such as widespread blackouts caused by AI-powered hacking or bot-engineered pandemics. As I spoke with the activists, I kept thinking about what had become of the climate movement—the Green New Deal passed, but only after being watered down, and it was then gutted by the second Trump administration—but their populist approach makes sense. Some of the biggest and perhaps only lasting successes over the past 15 years of American politics—the Tea Party, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, MAGA, and election denialism—have been fueled by outrage over an unfair economy and seemingly rigged politics.

These organizers have demonstrated their ability to win significant battles. Sunrise, 350.org, and others were instrumental in passing national legislation, galvanizing widespread climate demonstrations, and accelerating private-sector development of renewable energy. And Irreplacable’s members have already flexed some muscle when it comes to AI. In July, hundreds of people gathered for what was likely the largest anti-AI demonstration in San Francisco’s history, marching from OpenAI’s headquarters to Anthropic’s and finally to Google’s. A few months earlier, some of these “Stop the AI Race” organizers had staged a somewhat disorganized protest: Attendees at times struggled to chant in unison. The second time around, the march was advised by Ornstein, and attendees had chant sheets, a marching band, and a slushy truck (to “freeze” AI).

Already, a number of climate-oriented groups (including the environmental-justice arm of the NAACP as well as the Sierra Club and Earthjustice) are supporting local data-center battles by filing lawsuits, shaping model legislation, and organizing protests. The overlap is both concrete—data centers pollute the air and burn fossil fuels for their tremendous electricity demands—and thematic: a movement against corporate interests to change or regulate the technology of the future. At least on a local level, the groups are finding victories: Dozens of data centers have been canceled in the face of local opposition, and all of the major AI companies have promised to pay extra to avoid hiking up local electricity bills. In Michigan, both Abdul El-Sayed and William Lawrence, who is a co-founder of Sunrise, won Democratic primaries as progressive candidates hammering against data centers.

Still, this bubbling AI anxiety is far from a sweeping tide. That growing numbers of Americans are concerned about AI development does not mean they are concerned for similar or even compatible reasons. People may say they loathe data centers, but they might also enjoy the conveniences of AI products at home or work. They fear bots getting too powerful, too quickly, but also think America needs to stay ahead of China in AI development. At one anti-AI protest, I saw people who were ostensibly on the same side disagree about AI’s water use and whether certain jobs would be better off automated by chatbots. And to the extent that a sufficiently powerful AI movement would need to be global, just as climate organizing was, the technology generally polls much better outside the U.S. The AI backlash is to some extent an American phenomenon, which bodes poorly for any sort of global norms or treaties.

When pressed, nobody from Irreplaceable and no other climate activists turning to AI would articulate a concrete AI agenda. “We’ve aligned around saying no,” Lawrence recently told me. “Now, there is an important conversation that is yet to come, about—okay, so what do we want?” This is, for now, a significant weakness; a key turning point for the climate movement was providing a positive vision, the Green New Deal, for both decarbonizing and reinvigorating the American economy. Being able to link every data-center battle and primary campaign to a national vision would give the AI backlash some form.

It’s not wrong to want to develop a policy road map with the input of a broad coalition; climate advocates took decades to devise and unite around the Green New Deal. Irreplaceable’s stated plan is to build a coalition this year, develop a unified policy next year, and implement that agenda by the end of 2029. Measured against any metric other than Silicon Valley’s warp speed, that would be fast. But those few years will leave plenty of time for tech companies to push back—they’ve already spent tens of millions of dollars leading up to the midterms—and regardless, by then OpenAI, Anthropic, and any number of Chinese firms may already have built and lost control of even more powerful models.

Irreplaceable is wagering that people can move faster than capital. Absent specific policies, they are basically placing a big bet on populism—that the issue is not any particular chatbot or data center but the companies building them. The coalition comes first; the policy, after, Aroneanu told me. “You have to show the benefits to people immediately. It’s gotta land in their pocketbooks almost immediately for it to have political salience. And then you have to keep defending it.” Opinions about specific aspects of AI may differ, but fundamentally, people don’t like that “this technology is coming into their lives and they have very little control over it,” says Caroline Behringer, a communications strategist who worked on President Obamaʼs Climate Action Plan and now runs Athena Insights, a polling organization that studies attitudes toward AI. The movement, in Aroneanu’s words, must be polarized not left-right, but “down-up.”

Of course, Irreplaceable’s climate roots link it to progressive causes, and the group will primarily focus on organizing the center-left around AI. When I asked Aroneanu if he worried this might be counterproductive—polarizing the issue and allowing for the kind of partisan rancor and backsliding that beset climate activism—his response was pragmatic. “Chances are, this issue becomes polarized,” Aroneanu said. “I think that political parties are really exceptionally good at generating negative partisanship,” just as industry is likely to “split the base.” At some point, the climate movement had to decide that the best strategy was to accept partisanship and build power from the left. Although Irreplaceable hopes that conservative counterparts will emerge and believes its populist message will cross culture-war lines, Aroneanu does not see this as his explicit remit.

Broad, at times even ambiguous, backlash may make sense if AI is a general-purpose technology, as Silicon Valley is fond of saying—which is to say, if the technology touches and even upends nearly every aspect of the economy. Creating a technical oversight body for AI cyberattacks will not protect every American’s livelihood during mass layoffs; wealth redistribution will not prevent AI companies from spying on your most intimate interactions with a chatbot; voting won’t matter as much if AI companies become more powerful than Congress. Major figures at both OpenAI and Anthropic have suggested that a true AI revolution could require new democratic and economic institutions. Maybe they’re right. And maybe these companies, which have already torn down so much, should not also be the ones in charge of rebuilding.

entries.title: The Crisis for Democrats in Michigan
entries.summary: The Senate election presents liberals with a grim choice.
entries.content:
Updated at 4:34 p.m. ET on August 28, 2026

The hard-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker warned Jewish Americans last week that their excessive identification with Israel would subject them to anti-Semitic attacks. “If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action—not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews,” he said. Piker’s tone was one of rueful concern, not unlike the pose adopted by anti-Semites throughout history. “No person with a sense of the dignity of mankind can condone the persecution of the Jewish race in Germany. But no person of honesty and vision can look on their pro-war policy here today without seeing the dangers involved in such a policy both for us and for them,” the Nazi sympathizer Charles Lindbergh said in 1941.

Several leading Democrats, including Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, issued statements denouncing Piker’s ugly warning to the Jews as a barely veiled anti-Semitic threat. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat running for Michigan’s other Senate seat, trod more carefully. He issued a statement “in response to Hasan Piker’s comments” affirming that “all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence” and denouncing anti-Semitism, but the statement itself did not say whether Piker’s comment qualified as anti-Semitism. El-Sayed instead dismissed Piker as a distraction, saying at a recent rally, “The effort to make this race about a streamer in L.A. is actually kind of laughable.”

Most Democrats followed El-Sayed’s line that Piker was irrelevant. “This election is about what’s going to happen when we elect Abdul to the United States Senate. I am done, so don’t any reporter ask me again about Hasan Piker. It’s not what November is about,” Representative Debbie Dingell said at a rally for El-Sayed.

Democrats have good reason to say this. El-Sayed is running a close race to hold a seat that Democrats probably need to retain to win control of the Senate in the midterm elections.

But the truth is that Piker, and the uncomfortable questions raised by his alliance with El-Sayed, is one of the important questions at stake in the election. If Piker were just an internet pundit, his rant—the latest entry in a long list of outrageous comments he has made—would be of little consequence to the Democratic Party. Piker has said that “America deserved 9/11,” praised Mao Zedong as “one of the great leaders of this world,” and mourned the collapse of the Soviet Union as “one of the greatest catastrophes of the 20th century.” His ideology is profoundly authoritarian. But several left-wing Democrats, especially El-Sayed, have campaigned with Piker and elevated him into one of their most prominent surrogates. So El-Sayed’s alliance with Piker has become a political and moral crisis.

In Michigan, Democrats are trying to avoid handing Republicans their first Senate win in the state in more than three decades. But if El-Sayed wins, he would throw open the doors of the party to a strain of militant politics that many Jews justifiably consider dangerous. The Democratic Party is now divided between those who are trying to force El-Sayed to stop encouraging left-wing anti-Semites and those who give him their unconditional support.

The Michigan Senate election has presented liberals with a grim choice. The Republican candidate, Mike Rogers, has pledged support for a corrupt, racist, authoritarian-minded administration. Rogers hasn’t made even the tiniest concession to Donald Trump critics. But supporting El-Sayed means accepting a strain of anti-Semitic politics that to date has had no place within the Democratic Party.

What’s more, El-Sayed has already said that he intends to use his victory as a platform to reshape the party. Him winning could invite a future in which the United States has not just one party that is open to bigots but two.

Although El-Sayed has never said anything nearly as inflammatory as the sorts of comments Piker makes routinely, his mixture of anti-Zionism and populism treats pro-Israel activism as a nefarious and all-pervasive force. He has denied that any Democrat who believes in human rights could have any motive other than money for holding a position on Israel different from the one he prefers. El-Sayed tends to depict nearly all opposition to his candidacy as financially driven, but when applied to Jewish political activity,  this charge becomes even more conspiratorial.

Ann Arbor, where El-Sayed lives, is home to a branch of the Free Palestine movement that has engaged in violent intimidation of Jewish Democrats. Activists at the University of Michigan not only seized the central campus grounds for their own but also vandalized the business of Jordan Acker, a Democratic regent, and made middle-of-the-night attacks on his home, one of which involved shattering his window with a jar of urine.

El-Sayed has campaigned on the Michigan campus with Amir Makled, a lawyer who defended the protesters and who has shared anti-Semitic and pro-Hezbollah social-media posts. When the Justice Department charged eight of the protesters—one of whom had worked on El-Sayed’s campaign—in a plot to commit still more acts of intimidation, El-Sayed treated the indictment as biased, telling reporters, “It’s a lot more about what you’re advocating for that gets you indicted or not indicted, rather than what you did.”

Dana Nessel, the state’s attorney general, has faced anti-Semitic harassment and has said that she plans to skip the state party’s August convention rather than endure more abuse. At the party’s April nominating caucus, Mallory McMorrow, a then-candidate for Senate, reported that her Jewish husband was subjected to an anti-Semitic slur. On the weekend before the primary, Walter Masterson, a left-wing streamer who has appeared with El-Sayed, disrupted an event for Haley Stevens, El-Sayed’s pro-Israel opponent in the Democratic primary, forcing the brewery hosting it to cancel the event. El-Sayed did not condemn the bully-boy tactics used on his behalf.

Before he warned American Jews that they were bringing anti-Semitism on themselves by identifying with Israel, Piker displayed on his Twitch stream a quote attributed to Jeremy Moss, the Democratic nominee for Congress in a suburban Detroit district: “The entire purpose of my campaign is to make sure America continues to support Israel. I don’t think it’s wrong for Jews in America to want to put Israel first. America is not our homeland and we have been victims of antisemitism here.” Moss insists that the quote is a pure fabrication, and no one has yet produced any evidence of its authenticity.

Numerous Democrats denounced Piker’s comments. Instead of apologizing, though, Piker replied on X, “Aipac boss call was made,” implying that only the influence of the pro-Israel lobby could have caused Democrats to object to his rhetoric.

El-Sayed has refused pleas from his fellow Democrats to break off his alliance with Piker, who joined him at a pool party on the last day of campaigning before the primary. El-Sayed first brushed off the requests by likening Piker to Joe Rogan, a controversial podcaster whose show some Democrats have appeared on (but not a figure they have brought out on the campaign trail). More recently, he argued that the demands that he distance himself from Piker come from “cancel culture that all of us agreed was a bad idea back in 2020, but we seem to want to bring it back.”

This is a dodge. El-Sayed’s fellow Democrats are not trying to silence or punish Piker. They are asking El-Sayed, who chose to bring Piker out to campaign for and endorse him, to make clear where he stands. “Abdul El-Sayed had a prime opportunity to cut ties with Piker and directly disavow his words, but he did not,” Democratic Representative Hillary Scholten of Michigan told Politico. “There is a lot of work left to do to unite the party.”

Notably, El-Sayed is using an evasive construction similar to the one that J. D. Vance has employed to justify his friendship with Tucker Carlson. “We have far more important work to do than canceling each other,” the vice president told a conservative gathering last year. The reason Vance uses this deflection is obvious. He wishes to benefit from Carlson’s support without being held responsible for his ally’s most inflammatory claims. This has set off a bitter struggle within the right. Some Republicans are trying to throw Carlson out of the coalition; Vance wants to keep him in.

Democrats have little trouble understanding that the right-wing infighting over Carlson is about whether the Republican tent, which already includes racists, nativists, and vicious Islamophobes, is also big enough to include anti-Semites. They have correspondingly little trouble making harsh judgments about the moral compromises Republicans are contemplating in the process.

What many Democrats don’t wish to admit is that they are entertaining a similar choice themselves. El-Sayed and Piker have professed their abhorrence of anti-Semitism. But so has Vance—and, so, for that matter, has Carlson. If your opposition to anti-Semitism applies only to your ideological adversaries, and you excuse or ignore it from your allies, it is an empty bromide.

When Democrats dismiss the controversy over Piker and the movement he stands for, they are treating the growing influence of left-wing anti-Semitism as unworthy of concern—or, worse still, a fait accompli. The Democrats imploring El-Sayed to renounce Piker want more than a generalized promise to safeguard Jewish safety, or a statement that “nobody” speaks for the candidate. They are seeking some assurance from El-Sayed that he will speak out in opposition to attacks against Jews by his own supporters.

El-Sayed has responded as if the only reason Democrats might hesitate to endorse him is that they hold a personal grudge against him. “There are a few people who are still nursing wounds or grievances from the primary,” he told Semafor. “I get it. Losing is hard.” It is true that losing elections is hard. Losing your moral principles, on the other hand, can be surprisingly easy.

This article originally identified Hakeem Jeffries as the speaker of the House. He is the minority leader.

entries.title: The Sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln Deserve Better
entries.summary: The treatment of those on board betrays the promise made by the 16th president himself.
entries.content:
The treatment of those on board betrays the promise made by the 16th president himself.

When I was deployed at sea as a junior officer, I used milestones to track the passage of time. Each day counted toward something: a port call, when you get a break on land from the monotony at sea; the “crossing the line ceremony” when a ship crosses the equator (unfortunately, canceled at the last minute for my ship); and, eventually, the date I knew that, no matter what, I would be going home. Even on my worst days, that end point helped me stay focused on the mission and gave me something to be hopeful for.

The USS Abraham Lincoln left its home port of San Diego in November and was scheduled to return home in May. That did not happen. In the middle of this month, it surpassed more than 240 consecutive days at sea—one of the longest deployments on record—and had only a brief working port call early last month, where it appears sailors did not disembark, leaving them still at sea with land in sight. The 5,000 sailors and Marines on board have been working sustained combat operations, dealing with extension after extension and unreliable access to food, basic hygiene supplies, and mail.

The ship carries the name of a president who made a promise in his second inaugural address to care for people who have “borne the battle” and for their families. The treatment of those on board betrays that promise—and it is not limited to just this one ship on this one very long deployment. Rather, the crisis of the Lincoln has illuminated a pattern of callousness and cruelty toward military personnel, people who have sworn an oath to support and defend the Constitution of the United States of America. They have committed to going in harm’s way, but not to being neglected or treated with disrespect by the top of their chain of command.

The military used to understand that troops’ well-being was central to their ability to perform—and that improving the quality of life for those in the armed forces was not just a nicety, but a necessity. From 2021 to 2023, I served as acting director of force resiliency at the Department of the Navy, where I worked as part of an effort to support sailors’ and Marines’ mental health and reduce their suicide risk. Across administrations, both military leaders and career civilians have sought to foster a culture of respect throughout the armed forces. Some of that work was already ongoing during the first Trump administration: a shift toward prevention, building healthy command climates so that problems did not happen in the first place rather than being responded to only after the fact. Under the Biden administration, the Independent Review Commission on Sexual Assault in the Military produced ways to report sexual assault and harassment outside one’s chain of command, and provided independent investigators for those complaints. These efforts showed promise; sexual-assault and suicide rates have both fallen in recent years.

Sailors are resilient and try to make do with whatever they have. But that does not change the fact that on the Lincoln and elsewhere, they are at the mercy of poor planning, or no planning at all. Recent reporting from The New York Times and other outlets has shown that the Lincoln’s and other ships’ logistical issues could have been anticipated as far back as February, when the main base in Bahrain was damaged by an Iranian air strike, and resupply efforts were shifted to Diego Garcia, an island 2,200 miles from where carriers operate. This information was not made public, likely to save face and for operational security. Although Department of Defense leaders have had months to find alternatives, the administration does not appear to have planned for the conflict to stretch on this long.

The Navy needs more capable leaders; instead, an artificial leadership vacuum is being forced upon it from above. Throughout this year, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has been weakening the Navy’s leadership by blocking the promotion of nearly 20 admirals. He removed nine officers from the one-star-promotion list in May, and then seven more from the two-star list in July—by and large women and people of color who were selected by a board of their peers. Among those blocked from picking up a second star: Rear Admiral Amy Bauernschmidt, the first woman to command an aircraft carrier, by coincidence the USS Abraham Lincoln, which she led from 2021 to 2023. For the first time in more than a decade, no active-duty woman is likely to make admiral this year, and the subject is largely being ignored as a “woman problem” instead of being seen for the leadership crisis it is.

When families of the Lincoln’s sailors started talking with reporters, their complaints were met with contempt from the top. A Pentagon spokesperson, Sean Parnell, said that “legitimate challenges of a long combat deployment are being twisted into a false narrative,” and cited his own land-based combat deployment as evidence that the sailors needed to toughen up. Hegseth blamed “the reckless & shameless ‘American’ media.” The department’s rapid-response account answered reporting on food shortages by posting, twice, that sailors had ice cream. When asked whether the Lincoln’s deployment had gone on too long, President Trump’s response was to quip “not nearly long enough.”

I do not know what a junior enlisted sailor feels when they hear these comments. But there is a saying in the military that leadership sets the tone, and when the most senior leaders are flippant at best, and cruel at worst, many will understand that to be the permissible standard. The same leaders who so loudly demand that the country support the troops are not themselves doing so. And in June, this disrespect was put in writing: The Department of Defense issued a nonpublic memo on military equal opportunity and harassment that makes it easier for commanders to dismiss formal harassment complaints and retaliate against whistleblowers. Although service members do where they are told—and over the years, I have done many things while in uniform that I personally disagreed with—the respect of the commander in chief and military leaders is not supposed to be conditional. Most of their predecessors understood caring for those who go in harm’s way as a sacred obligation.

The USS Abraham Lincoln will come home. Another ship will relieve it. But homecoming is not just one day. For some sailors, the process will continue for the rest of their life. They will be expected to get back to business as normal: training, tending to the material condition of their ship, going to their new commands. They may also be moving to a new state (the Lincoln’s home port is planned to shift from San Diego to Bremerton, Washington), reconnecting with their families, and adjusting to a new pace of life. That is how the Navy operates.

The Navy’s SEAL teams have a cooldown period after deployment: time for family, therapy, whatever you need to be ready for next time. The rest of the Navy has no equivalent. Whether a sailor can tend to the home front or get counseling depends entirely on her immediate command, which is to say, on her boss. And for many, the check-engine light won’t show up for years. That was true for me. The PTSD from my three deployments and some traumatic noncombat experiences didn’t really show up until two years after I had left active duty, in part because I was no longer in the middle of it.

These sailors’ needs will then collide with yet another Trump-administration casualty: a weakened Veterans Affairs system. The VA eliminated nearly 30,000 positions last year. The War Horse reported on VA-medical-center policies that recommended discharging most patients from therapy after just eight sessions (far too few, according to many providers), an approach that the VA has denied adopting. The VA has lost more than 1,200 mental-health providers since the start of the administration, and demand is increasing. The department’s mission statement is President Lincoln’s promise itself. The bronze plaque outside its Washington, D.C., headquarters bears his words: “To care for him who shall have borne the battle and for his widow, and his orphan.” That’s not a promise the government is living up to today.

entries.title: A Wildly Popular Movie Meets the Film World’s Most Revered Label
entries.summary: KPop Demon Hunters’ inclusion in the high-class cinema catalog may signal a changing tide.
entries.content:
KPop Demon Hunters’ inclusion in the high-class cinema catalog may signal a changing tide.

Updated at 12:30 p.m. ET on Aug. 28, 2025

Over the past year, KPop Demon Hunters seems to have completely overtaken culture. Since premiering on Netflix in June 2025, the animated film has been watched nearly 650 million times and, according to Nielsen, accounted for some 20.5 billion viewing minutes last year. The soundtrack topped Billboard charts that fall; Spirit Halloween instantly sold out of licensed costumes.

But even the most ardent fans likely did not anticipate the mega-hit’s next big merch drop: a disc release from the Criterion Collection, home to some of cinema’s most distinguished titles. By some metrics, KPop Demon Hunters may be the most popular movie ever to be added to the collection. (Other new entries include David Lynch’s Wild at Heart and a Ukrainian folk romance from 1965.) It’s almost certainly the first Criterion inclusion to have its own flavor of McFlurry.

KPop Demon Hunters is an unlikely candidate for what’s come to be called “the Criterion treatment”: a painstaking transfer to disc, along with a making-of documentary and other special features, and a number printed on the box’s spine. Film buffs see this process as akin to an anointing; the trademark C, tucked into the upper-left corner of a plastic clamshell, signals a movie’s importance. Introducing a new title to the library can be fraught: James Kendrick, a professor of film and digital media at Baylor University, told me, “They’re always sort of risking diluting the power of that sign.”

Online, some of the label’s longtime devotees greeted the addition of KPop Demon Hunters with an eye roll, calling the move “substantially off-brand,” and a “cash grab.” The movie is so familiar to the general public that its release seems to go against the grain of Criterion’s reputation, which was built on bringing landmark works of film history to the masses. The company adds some 30 to 60 movies to its catalog annually, most of them lost gems of world cinema, festival-circuit darlings, or old Hollywood hits. In past decades, only one or two very new releases might have made the cut; canonization is usually a retrospective project of sifting through the past to see what art stands the test of time. Now the process seems to be speeding up: This year’s roster includes six movies from 2025 so far, many of them distributed by streaming companies.

Criterion has good reason to widen the net: Netflix, Apple, and Amazon make and distribute a significant share of films these days. A title that seems ubiquitous today could vanish tomorrow, evaporating from viewing platforms or even from personal digital libraries without warning. “We’ve lived kind of free and easy for the last couple decades, assuming these corporations would do that work for us,” Amanda D. Lotz, a media scholar at Queensland University of Technology, told me, “and that’s not in their remit, necessarily.”

Streaming services, unlike their traditional studio competitors, rarely produce physical media. “I suspect it is unclear that there is a market” for companion discs, Lotz said, despite the fact that, in her estimation, they could be a “nice little business niche.” (Signs are mixed: One by one, electronics companies have stopped manufacturing disc players, but the decline in disc sales seems to have slowed.) With more new films seeming transient—especially those whose rights belong to streaming studios—it makes sense for a label like Criterion to invest more in preserving them.

The decision to pick up KPop Demon Hunters also seems less surprising when you consider Criterion’s very early history. Back when the label was putting out movies on LaserDisc, in the 1980s, it was more inclined to pick up very new and popular titles, such as Ghostbusters. Some of that popcorn sensibility lived on in the brand’s DVD era, when it released Armageddon and The Rock, by Michael Bay.

Part of co-founder Bob Stein’s vision for the label was for it to distribute some titles that already had mass public appeal; Criterion, by offering a feature-packed disc to explore, could then deepen people’s relationship to those works and to the art form writ large. The brand has long been characterized by a high-low eclecticism: The literature scholars Mark and Deborah Parker told me that when they were working on their book about the history of the DVD, they visited Criterion’s office. Peter Becker, the president of Criterion, pressed a copy of a Japanese gangster flick into their hands; just down the hall, Mark told me, “they were doing the transfer of In the Mood for Love.”

The reasoning behind Criterion’s selections remains somewhat mysterious. (The company declined to be interviewed for this story.) Addressing an industry gathering in 2019, Becker said, “We let the movies carry the brand into the market place, so we don’t talk about the company very much.” But he did offer this explanation of what makes a work fit for Criterion: “It should be something we want to talk about, it should be a rich point of entry, but we try not to be snobby about what kinds of films can actually be exemplary.”

So what might KPop Demon Hunters exemplify? Its public reception has had a unique arc: a family-friendly fantasy that premiered on Netflix with little fanfare before becoming a word-of-mouth hit, then a critical darling, and finally an awards winner. As for its artistic properties, John Adkins, the lead writer for the newsletter Animation Obsessive, suggested to me that the film is “very tied to anime aesthetics and the slick, bright, Spider-Verse-type visuals that Sony Pictures Animation popularized” and that it could be taken to represent a modern-audience preference for an animation style with “a graphic or illustrative edge.” Tom Sito, a retired Disney animator and a professor emeritus at the University of Southern California, told me that the budding animators in his classes have adopted the movie the way he and his peers once did Yellow Submarine, the surrealist cartoon set to music by the Beatles.

That fervor might be enough reason to declare KPop Demon Hunters a contemporary classic and worthy of Criterion status. The revenue that it might bring in, which could then potentially fund more esoteric selections, is another. (Criterion, savvily, is releasing its edition just in time for holiday shopping, positioning it as an arty stocking stuffer.) Adding the film to the collection could be seen as part of a broader strategy to increase the company’s visibility, including through its “Criterion Closet” social video series, its mobile van, and a brick-and-mortar storefront during the Toronto Film Festival.

For many young fans of KPop Demon Hunters, who are more likely to pull up the “Golden” video on YouTube than pop a disc into a player, a souped-up Blu-ray might function mostly as a collectible—not so different from a Derpy Tiger plush or a Rumi singing doll. Some, though, may grow attached to the idea of physical media, or could even come to see home video as a vital technology rather than a nostalgia object. Cinema is a relatively young art form; the idea of owning a personal copy of a film is an even more recent invention. KPop Demon Hunter’s latest accolade is a reminder that the canon, too, remains far from fixed.

This article has been updated to reflect the nature of Criterion’s physical retailer.
